Part of that, I assume, is the way Ubuntu chased away a lot of the most vocal supporters they had in the past when they pursued interests that didn't necessarily have the communities support.

Also, in the last few years, I have seen Linux Mint being the recommended distro for newcomers. To be fair, the circles I run around are people that are already "nerdy" to begin with, and these suggestions are seen in IRC or support forums. So they obviously wouldn't be indicative of the average user experience. With computers being used more and more to simply access the internet, the simplest distros to migrate to get more recommendations, and power users move to something not Ubuntu (Debian, Arch, etc).

Although it seems the Linux user communities are forever at war with each other, it seems that they can all agree on one thing, don't use Ubuntu. Their focus seems to be on things outside of the desktop.

To be fair, that's probably by design. Canonical is probably looking at the future, and is less interested in desktop computing than ever before. I'm sure the adoption of so many computing devices that aren't desktops has influenced their focus since the original announcement.
